title: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library (imaginationlibrary.com)
comments: My daughter receives books through this program and I was curious how it was sustained at a $2.5/book wholesale cost.Interestingly, the coordinating body that selects books, facilitates distribution, and negotiates wholesale pricing is the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, but per-book funding is actually entirely through local charities and so on. This means that where charities are unable to act as partners, children will not receive books, but it also means that the program can operate by growing and shrinking as local support (including from state and local government grants) comes online and goes offline while keeping the overhead for local partners low.Dolly Parton came up with the initial local structure for her region in Tennessee and David Dotson of Dollywood scaled the operation using this decentralized model. Very impressive structure that makes this sustainable.Here’s the interview where he talks about it: https://www.endbookdeserts.com/dolly-parton-imagination-libr...reply

Regarding cost per unit. I think the publisher likes this type of partner because they can really get their initial order volume up high without much risk. This allows them to have a super low cost per unit, maximizing profit, from the start.reply
> initial order volumeNone of the books you get through this program are new releases. But they are printed special for imagination library.reply
Yup, and the “industry standard” wholesale discount publishers give to e.g. bookstores is usually 55%reply

That seems like an incredible discount. Can I assume then that bookstores are competing against each other via very minute (perhaps one or two dollar) price discounts while still maintaining a high profit margin?reply

I worked at a publisher back around 2010.The unit cost for the publisher to put a $20 AUD book on a shelf in a book shop was about $2 AUD.The bookstore kept quite a bit of that margin - $10 or so - but they had to pay rent & staff a store. If they were only selling $500 worth of books per day, it wouldn't have mattered if their margin was 100%, the fixed overheads would eat it all. If they could keep stock turning over quickly, the profits were impressive.reply

title: The State of Context Engineering (dbreunig.com)
comments: I like the idea of VictorTaelin's UniiChat [1] which summarizes every message into a single line and on top of that a binary tree of lines combined from lower levels. The context is then a view of that tree with more detail in recent messages and less detail in historical messages, plus a `zoom` tool that enables the agent to navigate the tree and read messages.An implementation of this idea based on the pi harness: https://github.com/jonaslsaa/pi-optchat[1]: https://gist.github.com/VictorTaelin/91837951a5ce5b38f341ec1...reply

It's nice that this article goes beyond the "context too long" scapegoat diagnostic.There is more to it than just reducing content in context. LLMs attention mechanism works by finding graphs of related words and concepts and it works best when the relevant relationships are close together in the text. Length matters but how well the information is organized matters as well.It's useful to be familiar with the concept of dependency length. The two sentences in this image ( https://benoitessiambre.com/img/dependencylength.png ) have the same words and same meaning but sentence C is organised to minimize the distance between related words.This can also apply to paragraphs and sections. Ordering them so that related information is recursively closer together, helps AIs think better (also helps humans, Dependency Length Minimization, DLM is an idea from psycho-linguistics).This is one reason progressive disclosure and sub agents are important. Including unnecessary information spreads apart surrounding information and makes it more difficult for AIs to figure things out.For eg. optimizing skills, it can help to put more important information at the bottom of a skill. Usually after a skill is loaded, the AI will start “thinking”, talking to itself to try to reason through a problem. The thinking block will have an easier time considering the text closest to it, the last part of the skill, than information farther up.Thinking blocks can produce a lot of text (a lot of it often hidden from users) that also spreads information apart. Sometimes, when an early instruction is still relevant but there’s been a lot of thinking and discussion added to the context since, it’s worth repeating a summary the early information ( keeping in mind that too many reminders can also spread other information apart ). I think however, LLMs are tuned to overweight very early information so that they don't disregard system prompts. You might be able to exploit this by placing some important facts near the very beginning of a conversation.If you've ever written compression algorithms where repeated blocks are referenced instead of encoded, you'll be familiar with how related information being clustered allows for better compression. It's another example of the parallels between intelligence and compression and it hints at the information theoretic aspect of DLM.reply

> As we focus more on memory, we also need to think about strategic forgetting. Over time, overly precise memories become conflicted and messy, and nobody has yet figured out how to handle this.> I think that’s the context problem of tomorrow.This passage is explains why humans have imperfect memory. Seems the perfect memory we wish LLMs had impedes creativity and is maladaptive.Strategic forgetting helps put the non-deterministic machine to best use. LLMs don't need perfect memory; that's covered by the computer itself.I like that this justifies the continuing relevance of context engineering - a seemingly dated term - in the face of trends like loop engineering.reply

title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis (lynchlab.net)
comments: This is an example of why I'm a little stumped about why people are excited about Jev-style decision models. For any application at scale it'd be way more accurate to have a dedicated classifier using the right architecture (neural net, bayesian, etc.) LLMs drive the cost of making those models down to near zero.Just use the LLM to make a thing that's actually good at what you need it to do.reply

Jev's launch was the best AI era marketing campaign I've seen so far. It was executed and timed so perfectly that Jev became synonymous with decision models overnight.I think it reveals how many people were only familiar with LLMs as the generic AI tool for everything. It only took one ambitious marketing campaign for someone to come along and present a simpler technology as a new breakthrough to audiences that hadn't considered anything else.The largest LLMs are really amazing for how much they can accomplish on unseen tasks. That is undeniably remarkable. The mistake that gets made everywhere is thinking that they're the best tool for every task, because LLMs are the only AI tool in most developer's AI toolbelt right now.reply

I think you have a very narrow and specific experience with people claiming to be "devs".I don't know of any devs in real life who would loudly and publicly get excited about anything unless it was their own completed project to show off.The tools are a footnote. It's precisely because it's so hard to get a project that far along that they would be familiar with many more tools than they would ever speak about. I suppose some people have a low bar. I wouldn't really call them "devs", especially now in this "AI era".reply

> I don't know of any devs in real lifeI think you're coming at this from a very narrow and specific experience with a few people you know.Jev really went from the announcement to being discussed all over overnight. We're discussing how popular things are in general, not among your narrow and specific group of people you work with.reply
I agree with what you said above, but not this. Jev was discussed "all over" by people chasing hype. I think that is actually a narrow set of people.reply
"No you!" :-)I think it's clear we're at the tail end of this cycle. I'm very glad to see it.reply

I think there are a lot of practical applications where something that works few-shot and doesn't require training is quite appealing if the cost of inference is low.  That's the sweet spot for Jev and similar models. If you have time and an eval set to train it, clearly a "real" special-purpose classifier should have much better performance (and for most applications cheaper cost/faster inference), but Jev and friends are way better than using a full-fat transformer LLM for a classification task.As an example, I've been using winnow running locally as a decision model in openchamber to select between llms for doing various tasks.  I don't have an eval set of different coding and other tasks that I could use to train a proper classifier.  This I just download off huggingface and it works out of the box and has cut my token spend to a fraction of what it was.  So it's good enough to be beneficial.reply

There are a lot of people working in software that have limited knowledge of information theory or machine learning.Unfortunately LLMs are magic to them.When you lack a first principles understanding of how something really works, you will bolt on hacks and duct tape on the wrong approach.reply

it's also the unfortunate practice of trying to use the new shiny thing everywhere and anywhere to signal that you're keeping with the times. It's funny how i've seen newer devs brush off things as 'traditional ml'reply

Which is nuts because one thing LLMs are actually pretty good up is generating "traditional ml" harnesses.  You just have to describe the problem you are trying to solve and ask the LLM for algorithm suggestions.It's also nuts because "traditional ml" generally requires a fraction of the resources of an LLM.  If you need to auto label, tag, categorize, it's never been easier to setup that sort of system in any project.reply

title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build (danluu.com)
comments: This statement stood out to me.> I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes.LLMs have hardened hundreds of apps where I work.Maybe it's a language-specific thing. Most of the time, in Java, LLMs take into consideration tradeoffs (especially if they are part of the initial prompt) and actively explains them. It generally won't make messy workarounds, without a lot of extra prompting forcing it to do so.Ofc, if you have:- Functional tests - you'll be able to see it in the execution times of specific APIs- Stress testing - performance profiling is the most important output artifactreply

> Maybe it's a language-specific thing. Most of the time, in Java, LLMs take into consideration tradeoffs (especially if they are part of the initial prompt) and actively explains them. It generally won't make messy workarounds, without a lot of extra prompting forcing it to do so.Claude in its current Opus 5.5 form has made some wild reaches in response to reasonable-seeming prompts. For instance: "this error is getting swallowed, make sure the real termination message exposes the root cause" -> discovering that the issue is actually in a third party library that isn't exposing the original error except so through logs, so doing some hackery to inject a log-capturer that gets the stdout, buffers it, and looks for the message in order to re-throw based on that...And it can demonstrate that working, but it's added some fragile and/or unintended consequences like (a) string matching on a particular WARN log message of a particular version of the lib, and (b) buffering those logs such that there were now cases where they would never make it to the actual output stream before the program terminating.It's certainly capable of being used smarter than that, but it's also really easy to end up with messy fragile stuff if you get lazy about reviewing the output.reply

> "this error is getting swallowed, make sure the real termination message exposes the root cause"Without judgement, I think this illustrates a fundamental objection the anti-AI crowd raises.The example prompt requires no understanding of what's happening, before suggesting action. Where I work, process requires that a PR review for a solution, has to have a corresponding explanation of why, or it's marked needs workreply

I don't disagree.I think there's some nuance here though between "fully anti-AI" and "be careful with that power saw."That example I mentioned didn't make it to production. It got noticed and fixed more properly by the person who submitted the first prompt before it even went to PR.But a lot of times things in that same vein can be solved sufficiently with a "dumb" prompt like that, so a one-line prompt to get a PR drafted in the background for the dumb stuff can be a pretty good time saver.The art is not skimping on your attention to the bigger or more important stuff so much that all the time you save on first getting code written is lost by cleaning up stuff like that...reply

As a very amateur woodworker in addition to my day job, I have always thought the power tool analogy is a good one for LLMs.  The tools don’t remove the need for skill and being very very careful with how you use them.  You can work faster but do a lot more damage also.reply
I think you're misunderstanding where in the process that prompt got made.reply

I used Opus 5.5 to figure out that a language model we were serving at work for internal use (we don't really serve models, we only use this internally because it processes sensitive data that we can't send to external endpoints) was being bottlenecked by CPU contention on tokenization, by having Opus run in an autoresearch style loop.Opus's first proposal for a fix was to spawn multiple Python processes and build a load balancer between them in Python. At first I asked it why it wasn't using haproxy and it said that haproxy would be an added dependency and that the overhead for this kind of thing in Python would be negligible. I knew this was idiotic but wanted to test this out, so had Opus run two experiments in parallel. Sure enough an haproxy load balancer was much, much better on HTTP load balancing than Python code was.This is the kind of thing that if you're unfamiliar with how networking code works, the models can autopilot into bad decisions that are verifiably correct (higher throughput than the original CPU-bottlenecked implementation) but much short of best practice.reply

Are you doing CPU inferencing? For small models you could check qxotic.ai which is a whole inferencing stack for many popular open models in Java, which can beat llama.cpp in speed in some cases. Its tokenizer toknroll is faster than tiktoken, which is what made me think of it for your use case.The advantage is that you don't have issues like the GIL or whatever, so there's no need for all the complexity of load balancing between multiple pythons.reply

Thanks for the pointers, I'm gonna look into them.I'm not doing CPU inferencing but I'm doing some tokenization in Python which is CPU-bound. In all honesty I started on this project to scale the model and did not build it myself so have been trying to read code and walk back the approach. I've been thinking about rewriting the Python glue in Go to avoid issues with the GIL.reply

> but it's added some fragile and/or unintended consequencesIn python, in a co-worker's code, it seems to significantly prefer "some_dict.get('key')" over "some_dict['key']".  For the non-python-users, the first one will return None (equivalent to null) when the key is missing, while the second raises a KeyError.  It was being used in a whole bunch of places that would cause problems (bad data instead of errors) if it did receive None.  Some of these keys were actually optional and it does makes sense for those, but it looks like whichever model he was using just repeated the pattern everywhere instead of just where it was appropriate.reply

And the question is competing with many other priorities in their inbox making it easier to snooze it for another day.This is not an excuse just an explanation. I was not aware of some of this until I got here. I try hard to answer thoroughly and with as much detail as possible. Sometimes it just takes a while.reply

Acoustic slow loris attack, lolreply

Like another commenter, I've also been on the other side, and there was open discussion about how to delay responses or leave incriminating information out of them.I remember specific examples of figuring out spurious legal objections to raise that would immediately fall if challenged, but would take months to challenge. I also remember people using records retention policies as 1) an excuse to destroy records that were still held, and pretending like they had been destroyed in the past, and 2) actively changing them in order to destroy things that had been requested, but maybe the request had been withdrawn to be resubmitted. I, as the IT person, remember being asked to come up with technical reasons why something could not be done, or would be expensive to do.Related: I remember my innocence as an eager little guy in one of his earliest professional jobs, installing a system that would make everybody's email easily searchable if a subpoena or a FOIA had to be responded to, and the sheer panic and chaos that ensued. The solution was to install a chat that instantly dumped history and was not searchable, and to have a lot more face to face meetings.Hanlon's Razor is a corruption enabler that only resonates because people confuse it with Occam's Razor. Occam was a logician; Hanlon's Razor was some bullshit submitted to a jokebook, and nobody knows who "Hanlon" is supposed to refer to.reply
